passages.context: Fortescue identifies the vimpa as the thin white silk scarf used by the two chaplains or servers who hold the mitre and crozier at pontifical functions. He compares it to a broad stole, says it is worn around the neck and tied in front, and says that the bearers hold the insignia through it. His footnote distinguishes the governing Ceremonial's express provision for the mitre-bearer's veil from the customary use of a similar veil by the crozier-bearer.

passages.context: Fortescue distinguishes three portable families. Acolytes’ candles are in tall footed candlesticks that can stand on the credence. Torches used by torch-bearers have no foot and cannot stand alone. The processional cross is fixed to a long staff and likewise cannot stand alone. These statements control functional distinction and support requirements, not material, dimensions, or ornament.

passages.context: In the general rules for pontifical servers, Fortescue gives the plural vimpae for the scarves of the mitre-bearer and crozier-bearer. If those chaplains wear copes, the scarf is under the cope. They hold the mitre or crozier through the scarf. The crozier-bearer transfers the staff directly to and from the bishop; the mitre-bearer transfers the mitre through the assisting deacon. The page also records distinct carrying orientations for each insignium.

passages.context: Fortescue places the credence and sedilia on the Epistle side in his teaching model. He describes the credence as the station for Mass vessels, books, and sometimes vestments when not in use; describes one three-place bench form for the celebrant and sacred ministers; and separately allows servers' seats on either side of the sanctuary or before the choir stalls. This controls recognition, liturgical relationship, and the distinction from server seating, not universal furniture construction, exact location, cloth drop, color, material, ornament, or architectural geometry.

passages.context: The seventh edition identifies the sacristy vesting table, says the priest washes his hands at the place prepared for that purpose, and directs him to bow his head toward the cross or principal image before following the server into the church. It separately reports as practice in many churches that the server rings a bell at the sacristy door to warn the people that Mass is about to begin. This supports a local/usual departure signal, not a universal rubric, one bell mechanism, one placement, or one operator in every church.

passages.context: Fortescue says the Roman custom does not carry a processional cross before the entrance when a priest sings High Mass and that the Roman ceremonial books therefore usually do not mention it. He adds that no rule forbids it and many churches customarily use it. When used, the cross-bearer carries it between the acolytes, places it in a convenient sanctuary stand on the Epistle side, and retrieves it for the recession. This supports optional/local status and the need for a stand; it does not make the cross Missal-required or universal.

passages.context: Fortescue’s torch-bearer section has the servers enter without torches, go to the sacristy around the Preface, take lighted torches there, and return at the Sanctus for the Elevation. The torches normally leave after the chalice elevation, but remain through Communion on identified occasions. A footnote expressly says that acolytes serving as torch-bearers use torches, not their candlesticks.

work.description: An English ceremonial manual first published by Adrian Fortescue in 1917 and repeatedly revised by J. B. O'Connell. It describes the ministers, appointments, vesture, and ceremonial execution of the Roman Rite. Printed page numbers are the conventional locus system; edition-specific claims must identify the exact revision consulted.
